bio: Hi! I’m Aryan 👋 I’m a Software Development Engineer at Amazon and a Computer Science student at Arizona State University. I enjoy solving complex problems, exploring emerging technologies, and turning ideas into useful software. I’m especially interested in AI agents and building systems people can rely on.

posts.title: The Engineering Behind Amazon’s AI Efficiency and Cost Savings
posts.excerpt: An Amazon SDE’s perspective on the engineering choices behind a faster, more cost-efficient ticket-classification system.
posts.body_html:
Screenshot from the Strands Agents case study.

As an SDE at Amazon, I’m excited to see teams turn advances in AI into practical improvements. A recent write-up from the Amazon Strands team is an encouraging example of how a well defined task and thoughtful engineering can make an AI system faster and more cost-efficient.

The team replaced Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider E4B for an internal ticket-classification workload. They reported model serving costs dropping from approximately $22,200 to $500 per million tickets, with average call latency falling from about 4.2 seconds to 0.9 seconds. Read their case study.

What stands out to me is the work around the model: adapting the inputs, evaluating the results, and planning the transition.

The engineers shortened category descriptions to fit a 4,096-token window and dropped older comments from longer tickets. They reported that E4B outperformed production Sonnet on a separate evaluation set. Implementation details.

Keeping the right context

Consider a ticket that might contain these two comments:

First comment: “Payments are failing because the service cannot authenticate to the payment provider.”

Latest comment: “Restarted the workers and increased queue capacity. The backlog is shrinking, but payments are still failing.”

If the first comment is removed, the remaining discussion could make the ticket look like a capacity problem. Preserving the root-cause information would help the classifier make the right distinction.

This is a useful scenario to test as part of an optimization: could the model give a confident answer when important context is missing? A confidence threshold won’t necessarily catch it.

This is an input contract question: when we change what reaches a component, how do we check that it still has enough information to do its job?

Building on a thoughtful rollout

The Strands team ran both models on live traffic before switching over and kept a configuration based rollback path. Rollout details. I appreciate that the team made comparison and recovery part of the transition.

One way I’d build on that approach is to give context truncation its own evaluation: compare classifications with and without the removed comments, inspect cases where the answer changes, and review high-confidence errors against independently checked labels.

The parallel comparison can surface disagreements; controlled follow-up tests can help explain whether they come from the model, the changed inputs, or both. That creates a practical way to keep validating the improvement as the workload evolves.

The team’s results are an encouraging example of matching AI capabilities to a specific job. For me, the opportunity is to carry that same care into the systems I build: pursue the efficiency gains, understand the inputs, and keep checking that the result serves the task.
